p: Gunpowder is a mixture of three things, none of them remarkable in itself: saltpetre, a white salt that forms in caves and dung-heaps and old cellar walls; sulphur, the yellow brimstone of the Bible; and charcoal. Mixed in the right proportions, roughly three parts of saltpetre to half a part each of the others, and touched with fire, they burn with such violence that the gases produced, confined in a tube, will hurl a ball of iron through the wall of a castle. It is a sobering thought that a large part of the history of the last six hundred years has turned on the proportions of a recipe.

Gunpowder was discovered in China, and, with an irony that Mr Gibbon would have enjoyed, it was discovered by men seeking the elixir of eternal life. The Daoist alchemists of the Tang dynasty, heating mixtures of minerals in their search for a medicine of immortality, found that certain mixtures containing saltpetre burst into flame. A text of about the middle of the ninth century, the Encyclopaedia reports, warns that some alchemists who had heated sulphur, realgar and saltpetre with honey had their hands and faces burnt and their houses burnt down. It was a hint which the military men did not ignore.

By the tenth century the Chinese were using gunpowder in war: at first in fire arrows, and in flaming bombs thrown by catapults. A military manual of ten forty-four, called the Collection of the Most Important Military Techniques, gives the earliest surviving recipes. Then came the fire lance, a bamboo tube full of powder fixed to a spear, which spat flame and fragments at the enemy; then, in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, tubes of metal firing projectiles, which are true guns. The oldest surviving gun, a small bronze hand cannon, is dated by the Encyclopaedia to about twelve eighty-eight. The Chinese used powder also for rockets and, in peace, for fireworks, which they have loved ever since.

Gunpowder and the gun travelled west in the thirteenth century, probably with the Mongols, who had learned them in their wars against the Chinese. By the middle of that century, the recipe was known in the Islamic world and in Europe. The English friar Roger Bacon, of Oxford, wrote about the year twelve sixty-seven of a children's toy made of saltpetre that made a noise like thunder. The first pictures of guns in Europe appear in an English manuscript of thirteen twenty-six, which shows a vase-shaped cannon firing an arrow at a castle gate. Edward the Third had a few cannon at the battle of Crécy in thirteen forty-six, though it was the longbow that won the day.

At first guns were small, unreliable and as dangerous to their users as to the enemy; King James the Second of Scotland was killed in fourteen sixty when one of his own cannon burst beside him. But in the fifteenth century, cannon grew large and powerful enough to change the conduct of war. High stone walls, which had made castles and walled towns almost impregnable for a thousand years, were easily battered down. The great walls of Constantinople, which had withstood every assault since the fifth century, were breached by the Ottoman guns in fourteen fifty-three. The King of France, invading Italy in fourteen ninety-four, took fortress after fortress in days which had formerly resisted for months.

The engineers responded, as engineers do, with a new kind of fortress, low and thick, with sloping walls of earth faced with brick and angled projections called bastions, from which guns could sweep every approach. Such fortresses were enormously expensive. So were the guns, and the gunpowder, and the large armies of infantry with handguns, called arquebuses and later muskets, that came to replace the armoured knight. Only a wealthy state with a strong treasury and an efficient system of taxation could afford them. Some historians therefore argue that gunpowder helped to destroy the independent power of the great nobles, who could no longer defy the king from their castles, and to create the centralised monarchies of early modern Europe. In the Middle East and India, the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires, which made great use of artillery, have been called the gunpowder empires.

Gunpowder was also an instrument of conquest beyond the seas. European ships armed with cannon could defeat almost any fleet they met, and bombard coastal towns at will, and the Spanish conquerors of Mexico and Peru, though their few guns mattered less than their horses, their steel and above all their diseases, carried them as a sign of terrible power. In the centuries that followed, a small number of Europeans with firearms came to dominate peoples many times their number in Africa and Asia.

The men of the future report that gunpowder itself was superseded, in the decades after my present year, by new explosives far more powerful: guncotton, already known in my day; nitroglycerine, made safe enough to handle by the Swede Alfred Nobel, who called his invention dynamite, and who, troubled by its uses in war, left his fortune to found prizes for peace and for science; and in the twentieth century, explosives so terrible that I shall postpone them to their place. The alchemists of the Tang sought a medicine that would let men live for ever. What they found has shortened more lives than any plague.
